name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
answer: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is a structured review of how an organisation's finance function actually uses artificial intelligence, covering the tools in play, the data they touch, and the controls around them. It sits inside governance, risk and financial data security work, and it is usually commissioned by a finance leader, an internal audit team or a risk committee rather than by the engineering group. The audit looks at both sanctioned systems, such as forecasting and reconciliation tools bought from vendors, and unsanctioned use, such as staff pasting ledger extracts into a public chatbot. Its output is a picture of where AI is running in finance, what it can reach, and where the gaps are.

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is a structured review of how an organisation's finance function actually uses artificial intelligence, covering the tools in play, the data they touch, and the controls around them. It sits inside governance, risk and financial data security work, and it is usually commissioned by a finance leader, an internal audit team or a risk committee rather than by the engineering group. The audit looks at both sanctioned systems, such as forecasting and reconciliation tools bought from vendors, and unsanctioned use, such as staff pasting ledger extracts into a public chatbot. Its output is a picture of where AI is running in finance, what it can reach, and where the gaps are.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the finance stack as it already exists: enterprise resource planning systems, the data warehouse or lake that feeds them, spreadsheets that still carry critical schedules, and the growing layer of AI features embedded in accounting and reporting software. It also has to account for the shadow layer, which is personal accounts on general purpose assistants, browser extensions and small scripts written by analysts. Evidence comes from identity and access logs, data loss prevention alerts, procurement records, vendor security questionnaires and interviews with the people doing the work. Nothing here requires a new platform, though a configuration management database or a data catalogue makes the mapping far less painful.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with an inventory: what AI is in use, who owns it, what data it reads and writes, and whether it makes or merely informs a decision. Each item is then assessed against the organisation's own policies and against the control frameworks the finance function already answers to, such as internal control over financial reporting and the expectations of external auditors. Practitioners trace data flows from source system to model output, test whether outputs can be reproduced, and check who reviews and signs off on anything that reaches a ledger or a disclosure. Findings are graded by the consequence of being wrong, not by the sophistication of the tool, and remediation is tracked like any other audit action.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on accountability: a named human owner for each AI system, a documented purpose, and a lawful basis for the personal and financial data involved. Provenance matters because auditors and regulators will ask where a number came from, which model version produced it, and what data trained or prompted it, so logs, version records and retention rules are part of the control set rather than an afterthought. Confidential financial data, client information and material non public information each carry their own handling rules, and cross border transfer adds another layer. The audit does not give legal advice, and questions about specific obligations belong with counsel and the compliance function.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the audit to move from an annual exercise toward continuous monitoring, with automated checks on which AI tools are connected to which data stores. Vendor assurance is likely to consolidate around standard questionnaires and model documentation, and finance teams will be asked to show evidence of human review on any AI assisted figure that reaches a filing. Regulation of AI in financial services is still developing in most jurisdictions, so the practical direction is toward traceability and clear ownership rather than toward any single standard. The teams that fare best are those that can answer, quickly and with evidence, what their AI systems do and who is answerable for them.
